Senses.Explanation: The first day opens the year's blessing. Liao'an Qingyu, Huiyue Xu, and Yushan Shangsi use the formula at New Year, commonly completing it with 'all things are renewed' before extending or questioning the seasonal greeting. Liao'an turns the formula into a short proclamation before willow and plum imagery. Huiyue joins it to stable mountains and rivers and the flourishing of the teaching. Yushan answers the public question about the renewed line with 'the grasses and trees give off light,' then repeats the formula in his address.

Senses.Explanation: This military maxim contrasts plentiful rank-and-file with the scarcity of one person capable of command. In Chan records it answers what happens when a sword leaves its scabbard, appraises a staff-bearing answer, and measures whether someone can carry a demanding encounter. Xuedou Zong answers the question about the sword after it leaves its scabbard with the maxim; Cuifeng Xian appraises Zhimen's staff that lifts sun and moon with the same contrast. Juelang Daosheng uses the line both when challenged about breaking his wish-granting staff and when speaking of meeting illness directly; Baichi Xingyuan places it after asking what to do with a person of the highest capacity, while Shengke Deyu contrasts the rare general with dead fire and cold ashes.

Xuedou Chongxian ends his verse on Sansheng and Yangshan's name-switching encounter with the line; Yuanwu Keqin asks why that famous laugh ends in this wind, while Shushan Ru uses it for a different case's verbal fall. The Tradition's Mirror Grove and the Record of Pointing at the Moon preserve Xuedou Chongxian's verse and Yuanwu Keqin's question about its last line. The Blue Cliff Record gives Yuanwu's extended appraisal of the same exchange. The Classified Anthology separately attributes the phrase to Shushan Ru in a verse on Yunmen's testing of an interlocutor.

Senses.Explanation: The thousand hands and eyes of Great Compassion are tested through questions about the true or principal eye. The “thousand hands and eyes,” attested 242 times in 108 texts, is the invoked form of Great Compassion, or Guanyin. Chushi Fanqi’s image record identifies it directly: “Great Compassion’s thousand hands and eyes are Guanyin’s responsive transformation-body” (大悲千手眼者，觀音大士應化之身也). In the Chan record the figure is repeatedly placed inside public interviews asking which is the “true eye.” Daowu asks, “Among Great Compassion’s thousand hands and eyes, which is the true eye?” and receives “like a person at night reaching behind for a pillow” (如人夜間背手摸枕子); the Magu–Linji encounter turns the same question into grabbing, demanding an immediate answer, and changing seats. A later teacher raises the whisk and says, “This is Great Compassion’s thousand hands and eyes” (此是大悲千手眼).

Senses.Explanation: Peach red, plum white, rose purple, yet when asked the spring wind knows none of it names distinct colours while withholding knowledge from the wind that brings the season. Jiqi Hongchu answers a house-founding challenge from a questioner whom the record does not name with the coloured flowers and unknowing wind. Wuyun Wu later raises the same line after contrasting an interlocutor whom his record does not name with his own account.

Senses.Explanation: Wuyun Wu points to red peach, white plum, and purple rose, then says that the spring wind knows nothing when questioned. Distinct colors appear through spring without the wind offering an explanation. Wuyun Wu gives the line after contrasting ordinary acts of seeing with a claim not to see. Biefeng Zhen gives it after saying the upward road is not transmitted by the sages. Nanyue Jiqi answers an unnamed questioner's challenge about establishing a house with it and then rejects the congratulation.
